method: The fragment was written and first refuted with no web search at all (the run's shared allowance was spent), resting on the Codex's library and the writers' memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and their dates, the classification and its decree, the sites, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned; every source is read: search, from the producer's or the appellation body's own domain where marked primary (Leflaive, Comtes Lafon, d'Angerville, Bouchard, the Bourgogne wine body, the appellation's rules, the Climats body). The Lafon pages were returned at http addresses and are given at https, as the lint requires.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (Inside Burgundy, Wine with Seth, a critic's pages) was read as a lead and never cited.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches.

The family in Puligny since 1717: the domaine's own pages: confirmed as the domaine's claim; founded stays empty, since 1717 is the family's presence and the domaine took shape between 1905 and 1930.

The sons from 1953 to the early 1990s (Wikipedia and a merchant): confirmed; the father's birth year, 1921, found in no source (a civil death record of another man of the name gives 1924 to 1988), his death in 1993 only on two writers' own sites: he is no longer named.

The site: Chevalier-Montrachet at 265 to 290 metres against Le Montrachet's 250 to 270 and Bâtard's 240 to 250, thin, stony rendzinas on marls and marly limestones, wholly in Puligny, white only, the decree of 31 July 1937 (the Bourgogne wine body's pages): confirmed; directly above and deeper soils were more than the sheets say.

changed.was: Generations of Leflaives had farmed in Puligny, but the domaine took its shape in the early twentieth century, when Joseph Leflaive (1870 to 1953), an engineer, came home to the village after phylloxera and bought vineyards one by one. After his death his sons ran the domaine together, among them Vincent Leflaive (1921 to 1993), and they made its name abroad as the reference for Puligny's precise, stony whites. In 1990 Vincent's daughter, Anne-Claude Leflaive (1956 to 2015), came to share the direction with a cousin and soon led it alone. She began trials of biodynamic farming in the vineyards and by the late 1990s had turned the whole domaine over to it, an early convert among the great domaines of Burgundy. In the early 1990s the domaine added a small parcel of Le Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet is the wine it leads with: its parcel sits on the thin, stony upper slope, above the deeper soils of Le Montrachet and Bâtard, and gives a narrower, more chiselled wine than either. Les Pucelles, the premier cru, is the bottle a guest meets more often; the Chevalier is the house's grand cru measure. Its virtues are line and patience, and it asks the same of whoever opens it.
changed.now: The Leflaive family has been rooted in Puligny since 1717, by the domaine's own account, but the domaine took its present shape in the early twentieth century, when Joseph Leflaive (1870 to 1953), a naval engineer, came home to a village whose vines phylloxera had laid low. He bought vineyards one by one and replanted them on grafted rootstocks, parcel by parcel. After his death in 1953 two of his sons ran the domaine together until the early 1990s. In 1990 the daughter of one of them, Anne-Claude Leflaive (1956 to 2015), came to share the direction with a cousin and began biodynamic trials on a small plot; from 1994 she led the domaine alone, and in 1996, by the domaine's own account, she put the whole estate under biodynamic farming. In the early 1990s the domaine also added a small parcel of Le Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet is the wine it leads with: its parcels sit on the stony upper slope above Le Montrachet, well above Bâtard lower down, and give a narrower, more chiselled wine than Bâtard. Les Pucelles, the premier cru beside Bienvenues, is the one argued for promotion; the Chevalier is the house's grand cru measure. Its virtues are line and patience, and it asks the same of whoever opens it.
changed.why: Joseph Leflaive's dates, his work as a naval engineer, his purchases and replanting after phylloxera, the sons until the early 1990s, Anne-Claude Leflaive's dates, the shared direction from 1990 and her sole charge from 1994, trials on a small plot in 1990 and the whole estate biodynamic in 1996 (1997 in other accounts, so the year is the domaine's) as the sources give them; her father's birth year, 1921, was found nowhere and his death year only on writers' sites, so he is no longer named; made its name abroad and an early convert among the great domaines were claims of rank, cut; Le Montrachet's and Bâtard's soils are no longer called deeper, which the wine body does not say; Bâtard is placed by the altitudes it gives.

changed.was: The domaine's founder married into Meursault in the 1890s and gathered vineyards in its well known climats, Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes among them, with a parcel of Le Montrachet and the walled Clos de la Barre around the family house. In 1923 he revived the Paulée de Meursault, the feast that closes the harvest, and later added to it a literary prize paid in bottles of Meursault. After his time the family let most of its vines to sharecroppers, who farmed them for a share of the crop, and the domaine bottled only part of its own wine. In 1984 the founder's great grandson took charge and over the following years brought the vineyards back into the family's own hands; from 1998 he farmed them biodynamically, and in 1999 the family began a second estate in the Mâconnais, the Héritiers du Comte Lafon. Meursault has no grand cru, and Les Perrières, stony ground above Les Charmes, is the premier cru most often argued for promotion. In Lafon's cold cellars it gains breadth without losing its line. Meursault is often sold on richness alone; this wine shows it can be precise as well.
changed.now: The founder was no Burgundian: born in the Tarn-et-Garonne in 1864, he was an inspector of the public registry, and in 1894 he married into the Boch family, merchants and growers of Meursault. The domaine grew from his wife's inheritance and from later purchases and exchanges, and came to hold Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, the walled Clos de la Barre around the family house and a parcel of Le Montrachet. In 1918 the Holy See made him a papal count, in thanks for his refusal, as an inspector, to make the clergy declare their wealth, and the domaine's name carries the title. In 1923, as mayor of Meursault, he revived the Paulée, the feast that closes the harvest, inviting thirty five friends to dine in his vat room. After his death most of the vines were let to sharecroppers, and in 1956 his grandson stepped in to stop the domaine being sold. In the mid 1980s the founder's great grandson took charge, ended the last sharecropping leases by 1993, farmed biodynamically from 1998 and in 1999 bought a second estate in the Mâconnais, the Héritiers du Comte Lafon. Les Perrières, stony ground towards Puligny, is the premier cru most often argued for promotion, and here it gains breadth without losing its line.
changed.why: The founder's birth in 1864, his post in the registry, the marriage of 1894, the inheritance and later purchases, the papal title of 1918 and the Paulée of 1923 with thirty five friends in the vat room are the domaine's own history; his death year was found nowhere, so he is described, not named; the literary prize was found in no source and is cut; the sharecropping, the grandson in 1956, the great grandson in the mid 1980s (accounts give 1983, 1984 and 1985, so 1984 is softened), the last leases by 1993, biodynamics from 1998 and the Mâconnais in 1999 rest on two accounts each; the founder's own purchase of the Le Montrachet parcel is no longer claimed; the closing line on richness alone is cut for length.

changed.was: The hill of Corton carries the name of Charlemagne (about 747 to 814), who, the story goes, held vines there, and in 775 gave land on the hill to the abbey of Saulieu. A later legend says white grapes were planted on his part of the slope so that red wine would not stain his beard. The hill's white wine kept his name, and in 1937, when the appellations of the Côte de Beaune were drawn, Corton-Charlemagne became a grand cru spread over three communes, with Corton, the red, below it. Coche-Dury is a small Meursault family domaine whose name joins two families, Coche and Dury, by a marriage of the 1970s. Its wines, from Bourgogne Blanc to the grand cru, are made the same way: long lees ageing in barrel and a deliberate reduction that gives a struck match note over citrus and salt. The style spread far beyond Burgundy, and the domaine passed to the next generation in 2010 without changing it. The Corton-Charlemagne comes from a small parcel and is made in very small quantity. Keep it, and when its time comes, keep a decanter beside it.
changed.now: The hill of Corton carries the name of Charlemagne (about 747 to 814), who held land there and in 775 gave much of the hill to the abbey of Saint-Andoche at Saulieu. A later legend says white grapes were planted on his part of the slope so that red wine would not stain his beard. The hill's white wine kept his name, and on 31 July 1937 a decree made Corton-Charlemagne a white grand cru spread over three communes, with Corton, the red grand cru, sharing the hill. Coche-Dury goes back to a grower who worked vines in Meursault in the 1920s; his son began to sell wine under the family's own label in 1964, and in the 1970s a marriage in the next generation joined the names Coche and Dury. Its wines, from Bourgogne Blanc to the grand cru, rest long on their lees in barrel, with a deliberate reduction that gives a struck match note over citrus and salt, an approach that spread far beyond Burgundy. The domaine passed to the next generation in 2010. The Corton-Charlemagne comes from a small parcel and is made in very small quantity. Keep it, and when its time comes, keep a decanter beside it.
changed.why: The gift of 775 was to the abbey of Saint-Andoche at Saulieu, as Wikipedia and Decanter give it, and Charlemagne held the land rather than vines by a story; the decree of 31 July 1937 is the appellation's own; Corton is on the same hill, not simply below, since some parcels may be declared either; the domaine's roots in the 1920s and the label of 1964 rest on Wikipedia and two merchants, the marriage of the 1970s on all of them (1975 in most); without changing it was a claim no source made and is cut; made the same way becomes the long lees and the reduction the library gives.

changed.was: The Dukes of Burgundy, the story goes, kept vines at Volnay, and the walled vineyard beside the village took their name. In 1804 a forebear of the family bought the estate, and it passed by descent to the Marquis d'Angerville. In the 1920s the Marquis of the day took on the merchants: he denounced the fraud by which wine from elsewhere was sold as Burgundy, was shut out by the merchants for it, and answered by bottling and selling his own wine at the domaine, among the early growers of the Côte d'Or to do so. His stand fed the appellation laws of the 1930s. His son ran the domaine for half a century until his death in 2003, and the family's own selection of Pinot Noir, known as Pinot d'Angerville, was planted well beyond Volnay. The next generation took charge in 2003, turned the vines to biodynamic farming and in 2012 founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura. Clos des Ducs is the heart of the domaine: a monopole beside the house, and a Volnay premier cru argued for promotion. In the glass it makes Volnay's case: perfume and line rather than weight.
changed.now: From the twelfth to the fifteenth century, by the domaine's account, the Dukes of Burgundy held the vineyard beside Volnay that carries their name. In 1804 a forebear of the family, then sub-prefect of Autun, bought the Clos des Ducs estate, and in 1888 a later heir left it to his nephew and godson, then fifteen, the future Marquis d'Angerville. Phylloxera had ruined the vines, and from 1906 the Marquis, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts rather than in a cellar, replanted them with fine Pinot Noir. In the 1920s he spoke out against the blending of some Beaune merchants; they stopped buying his crop, and he answered by bottling and selling his own wine at the domaine, among the early growers of the Côte d'Or to do so. His stand fed the appellation laws of the 1930s. His son ran the domaine from his father's death in 1952 until his own in 2003, and the next generation turned the vines to biodynamic farming from 2006 and in 2012 founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura. Clos des Ducs, which the domaine calls its grand vin, is a Volnay premier cru argued for promotion. In the glass it makes Volnay's case: perfume and line rather than weight.
changed.why: The Dukes from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, the sub-prefect of Autun in 1804, the bequest of 1888 to a godson of fifteen, the replanting from 1906 and the Beaune trade ceasing to buy his crop are the domaine's own history; boycott and fraud were stronger than the domaine's words and are softened; 1952 and 2003 rest on two merchants; biodynamics from 2006 is the domaine's; the Pinot d'Angerville selection planted far beyond Volnay was confirmed in no source and is cut; the Marquis and his son stay undated, so they are described, not named.

picks.ruling: kept: the domaine's own pages and the library call Chevalier-Montrachet its grand vin, and the house list carries it; Les Pucelles is first among the others.
kept: Les Perrières is the premier cru the domaine and its merchants show first, and the domaine's own site carries a vertical of it.
kept: Corton-Charlemagne is the domaine's one grand cru; its Perrières is taught in Lafon's record. The plan's why calls it the rarest bottle a list may hold, a claim the record does not repeat.
kept: the domaine calls the Clos des Ducs its grand vin and holds it whole.
kept: Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus is the house's historic signature in the library, and its own site sets it among the wines it names first.

codexInTension.says: Volnay Caillerets Ancienne Cuvée Carnot: Premier cru monopole in Volnay
codexInTension.found: The house calls it the plot of its first purchase, in 1775, in Les Caillerets, named for the Carnot family who once owned it; Caillerets is shared, and the house never calls the wine a monopole. Its own holdings line calls it a cuvée.

sources.title: Bouchard Père et Fils: Volnay Les Caillerets
Bouchard Père et Fils: The wines

codexInTension.says: a rare case of a negociant holding two Côte de Beaune monopoles
codexInTension.found: Clos de la Mousse is a monopole whole since 1872; Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus is a parcel held whole within the shared Les Grèves, and the house's site also carries a Beaune Clos Saint-Landry, which the first refuter took for a further monopole; the count of two was not searched and is not settled.

sources.title: Bouchard Père et Fils: Beaune Clos de la Mousse
Bouchard Père et Fils: Beaune Les Grèves

codexInTension.says: Deliberate reduction, long lees ageing and old barrels; Corton-Charlemagne a few barrels a year, the rarest wine in the range
codexInTension.found: Every account read gives a share of new barrels, rising for the top crus (a quarter to a half), fifteen months to two years in barrel and bottling without filtration; the rarest wine was not settled.
